desc:
Given two integers lo and hi, return the bitwise XOR of every integer from lo to hi inclusive: lo ^ (lo + 1) ^ ... ^ hi.

The range can be long, so do not loop over it.

lo = 1, hi = 3  -> 0   (1 ^ 2 ^ 3)
lo = 2, hi = 4  -> 5   (2 ^ 3 ^ 4)
lo = 0, hi = 5  -> 1
hints: Compute the XOR of 0..n for small n by hand. Do you notice a pattern that repeats?
Let F(n) be the XOR of 0..n. Then the XOR of lo..hi is F(hi) ^ F(lo - 1), because the numbers below lo cancel out.
F(n) is n when n % 4 == 0, 1 when n % 4 == 1, n + 1 when n % 4 == 2, and 0 when n % 4 == 3. Let F(-1) = 0.
editorial: XOR cancels equal values, so the XOR of 0..n depends only on n modulo 4. Pairing up the numbers as (4k+1, 4k+2)-style blocks shows that each block of four consecutive numbers starting at a multiple of four XORs to zero. What remains is the last few numbers, which gives the four cases of F.
Because XOR is its own inverse, the XOR over [lo, hi] equals F(hi) XOR F(lo - 1). Each query costs constant time regardless of how long the range is.
